tests.name: Zoom out from the Jalama Creek Segment without exposing an empty flat-color coastal void.
tests.methodology: Opens the locally served page in test mode and waits until the test seam reports ready and SceneView has finished loading with a still camera. The browser page, ArcGIS SceneView, and committed published creek data are real. Preserve Aerial Imagery Overlay, Esri World Imagery, and Esri World Elevation responses are real and are reused from a local disk cache; a response missing from the cache is fetched live and saved. When a live fetch fails with DNS, TLS, HTTP 429, or HTTP 5xx and no frame failed, or no terrain tiles arrive, the result is inconclusive rather than passed. Nothing else is mocked. After the opening frame, the test-mode camera command moves the camera instantly to a fixed coast-scale pose about 12 km up, the pose three mouse-wheel notches reach, and waits again until the scene has finished loading. At the opening frame and the coast frame it screenshots a 640×480 clip of the scene, masks the sidebar using its DOM bounding box, samples every fourth pixel, and fails when the share of those pixels whose RGB exactly equals the single most common RGB exceeds 10%. A measured flat-color failure stays a failure even when Esri also reported an outage. The failure names the step, camera height, flat color, and share, and attaches the screenshot. It does not check mouse-wheel input, intermediate zoom levels, a white far-zoom frame, imagery sharpness, tile vintage differences, terrain accuracy, or water appearance. Imagery dataset used in the visualization: Jack and Laura Dangermond Preserve Aerial Imagery - 2024 (8 cm, January 2024, via Vandenberg), over Esri World Imagery outside the Preserve.
tests.rootCauseAnalysis: Symptom: zooming out from the Jalama Creek Segment exposes an empty flat-color coastal void. Root cause: old USGSImageryOnly transparent coastal tiles let the navy ground color show through. Red evidence: commit cac781c measured 34% flat navy in the optimized crop; fixed coast frames stay at or below 4.4%. Fix: Esri World Imagery replaces those transparent coastal tiles. Future triage: if a coast frame is flat navy, inspect imagery tile transparency and ground show-through before treating the frame as an imagery outage.

tests.name: Zoom across the Jalama creek scene without raising tile-shaped terrain slabs.
tests.methodology: Opens the locally served page in test mode and waits until the test seam reports ready and SceneView has finished loading with a still camera. The browser page, ArcGIS SceneView, and committed published creek data are real. Esri World Imagery and Esri World Elevation responses are real and are reused from a local disk cache; a response missing from the cache is fetched live and saved. When a live fetch fails with DNS, TLS, HTTP 429, or HTTP 5xx and no frame failed, or no terrain tiles arrive, the result is inconclusive rather than passed. Nothing else is mocked. It checks three settled frames: the opening frame; the slab camera, where the old custom elevation layer drew 100% missed ground rays (camera at about -120.474, 34.502, 1,245 m up, heading 321°, tilt 58°); and a wide camera about 12 km up. The test-mode camera command moves the camera instantly to each fixed pose and the test waits until the scene has finished loading. Each frame samples an 8×8 grid in the central scene through sampleRenderedGroundHeights, which uses SceneView toMap on the drawn ground and not ground.queryElevation. The grid stays right of the sidebar and below the outer horizon band so the fixed Esri scene returns terrain hits. The test fails when more than 20% of those samples are null, when any non-null height is outside -20..2500 m, or when at least 6 edge-contiguous samples form a block whose elevation range is under 1 m, whose median is more than 120 m above the median of the adjacent ring, and whose samples span more than 200 m on the map. A measured terrain failure stays a failure even when Esri also reported an outage. Failure messages include the measured null share, heights, and plateau figures. It does not check mouse-wheel input, intermediate zoom levels, the return to the opening camera, exact terrain accuracy, imagery appearance, sharpness, vintage, ocean flatness, or water placement. Imagery dataset used in the visualization: Esri World Imagery.
tests.bugReference: lifted tile-shaped terrain slabs during zoom
tests.rootCauseAnalysis: Symptom: a large photographic square appears lifted high with vertical walls during zoom. Root cause: old custom Usgs3DepElevationLayer.fetchTile returned a plain {values,width,height,noDataValue,usedMemory} object instead of new ElevationTileData(...); ArcGIS received undefined minValue/maxValue/hasNoDataValues, so terrain mesh bounds became invalid/NaN and tiles drew as vertical walls. Raw 3DEP heights were valid (about 0–330 m), so source-height queries false-passed. Reproduction baseline: git commit cac781c, old USGS scene, viewport 1440×900, wheel at (893,495), deltaY 420; by notch 3 the camera was about (-120.474, 34.502), z about 1245 m, heading 321°, tilt 58°; rendered view.toMap samples were 100% null while source elevation was 0–328 m. Fixed-environment evidence: returning actual ElevationTileData made samples 0% null at that camera; the current fix removes the custom layer and uses Esri World Elevation. Future failure triage: first inspect the rendered toMap hit rate and any custom ElevationLayer fetchTile return type or metadata; then inspect similar mesh-bound failures; only after that investigate source elevation values.

tests.methodology: Opens the locally served page in test mode and waits until the test seam reports ready and SceneView has finished loading with a still camera. Preserve Aerial Imagery Overlay, Esri World Imagery, and Esri World Elevation responses are real and are reused from a local disk cache; a response missing from the cache is fetched live and saved. tests.bugReference: far-zoom white scene caused by the local view far clip
tests.rootCauseAnalysis: Symptom: zooming far out clears the scene to an all-white frame, and zooming back in does not reliably recover it. Root cause: the old local SceneView constraints.clipDistance.far of 80000 cleared the frame once view rays exceeded the 80 km far clip. Red evidence: baseline commit cac781c; the optimized crop measured 92% flat white. Fix: a global SceneView with no 80 km far clip. Future triage: compare camera altitude with the view clipping constraints before investigating an imagery outage.

tests.name: Clicking the creek scene does not draw a (usually light blue) focus frame around the view.
tests.methodology: Loads the Esri dark theme and the app stylesheet, in that order, on a local page whose only view markup is an .esri-view containing a focusable .esri-view-surface. SceneView, the map, imagery, terrain, and the network are absent. The test clicks the surface and reads the computed outline of its ::after pseudo-element. It fails when that outline has a non-zero width and a painted style. It does not check keyboard focus, widget rings, water, or camera navigation.
tests.rootCauseAnalysis: Symptom: clicking the creek scene paints a light-blue frame around the whole view. Root cause: the Esri dark theme draws that frame on .esri-view .esri-view-surface:focus::after as a 2px solid Calcite brand outline, offset -2px. Calcite is Esri's design system. The surface is focusable, and its own outline is already 0, so resetting the element outline misses the frame. Reproduction: before the fix, the clicked surface ::after outline measured 2px solid rgb(0, 122, 194). Fix: the app stylesheet clears that ::after outline for pointer focus and leaves the keyboard :focus-visible ring. Future triage: after a click, inspect the surface ::after computed outline width, and confirm the app stylesheet still loads after the Esri theme.

tests.name: Looking up from below the water surface, the water-surface polygon fills the view and does not leave a hole exposing the bank terrain beyond.
tests.methodology: Opens the locally served page in test mode and waits until the test seam reports ready and SceneView has finished loading with a still camera. Pins Creek Segment 27714637-026's water-surface elevation to 26.50 m through the test seam, confirming via segmentPlacements that the active bucket's minimum reads 26.5 m. Moves the camera instantly to a fixed below-water, upward-looking pose at (-120.48482532, 34.51368790, 26.037 m), heading 342.70°, tilt 95.47°, and settles the scene. For each of a captured hole ground point and a captured known-good ground point on segment 27714637-026 at water-surface elevation 26.50 m, projects the WGS84 point to a screen pixel through the test seam and calls hitTestAtScreen on that pixel. The test fails when hit-testing either point returns no water-surface hit on segment 27714637-026, or when the returned bucket minimum is not 26.5 m. The browser page, ArcGIS SceneView, and committed published creek data are real. Esri World Imagery and Esri World Elevation responses are real and are reused from a local disk cache; a response missing from the cache is fetched live, and if that fetch is unavailable the result is inconclusive rather than passed. Nothing else is mocked. It does not check pixel color, polygon area, exact rim position, or the behavior of any other segment. Imagery dataset used in the visualization: Esri World Imagery.
tests.bugReference: water-surface polygon rim leaves a hole exposing the bank terrain beyond
tests.rootCauseAnalysis: Symptom: at a below-water, upward-tilt camera over Jalama Creek, visible holes appear along the water-surface polygon rim; a view.hitTest through one of those holes returns zero water-surface hits and resolves on the bank terrain beyond. Root cause: 1 m USGS 3DEP cell quantization produces a stair-stepped waterline where the water surface meets the bank; without an outward dilation of the wet mask before the contour is traced, the polygon rim sits exactly on those raster cells, leaving sub-cell gaps between the polygon edge and the real bank. Low- and upward-tilt camera rays find those gaps. Red evidence (2026-10-15, segment 27714637-026 at WSE 26.50 m, camera -120.48482532, 34.51368790, 26.037 m, tilt 95.47°): hitTest at the hole ground point (-120.48485151, 34.51378253) returned hits=[]; at the adjacent known-good ground point (-120.48483593, 34.51372363, z 26.5) it returned one water-surface hit for segment 27714637-026 at bucket 26.5–26.55 m. Fix: BANK_OVERLAP_MARGIN_M = 2 in pipelines/creek-visualization-data-production/constants.ts dilates the wet mask by 2 cells before the contour is traced, bounded by the Creek Segment corridor so it cannot bleed into a neighbouring creek. Future triage: at a low- or upward-tilt camera over the creek, a hitTest returning zero water-surface hits on a pixel where a known-active segment should cover points first at the bank-overlap margin or the WSE publishing pipeline before anything else.

tests.name: No stair-stepping (proper water polygon slanting): Modeled water at a low-flow hour shows no stair-stepping between neighbouring Creek Segments — clicking the creek bed at the segment boundary returns a water-surface hit.
tests.methodology: Why it matters: on a sloping creek a person should see water follow the bed down from one Creek Segment into the next, not flat steps with dry ground between them. How it checks: opens the locally served page on the “Inferred Creek WSE — hourly (from NOAA National Water Model v3.0 flows)” Dataset for the dangermond-preserve extent at 2017-10-01T00:00Z (Sep 30, 2017, 5:00 PM PDT), a low-flow hour, waits until the test seam reports ready and the modeled seam has finished loading, and checks that the opening time matches the URL. The test-mode camera command then moves the camera instantly to the developer's saved oblique pose looking up side creek 27714697 (Creek Segments 043 and 044), where flat water terraces float as separate steps above the sloping bed, and the test waits for the modeled loads to finish and for the scene to finish drawing with a still camera. It replays three creek-bed clicks the developer captured with the dev tools from that pose, where water was expected and none was hit. Each click is stored as the ground point SceneView reported under the cursor, projected back to a screen pixel at run time so the check does not depend on viewport size, and SceneView.hitTest runs there. The test fails when any of the three pixels has no water-surface graphic. The failure message gives the click location, its nearest Creek Segment, the clicked ground height, the drawn surface height, the modeled water-surface elevation the page holds for that segment, and the other layers hit. What is real: the browser page, ArcGIS SceneView, the local pipeline output served by the development middleware, and Esri World Imagery and Esri World Elevation responses reused from the local disk cache; a response missing from the cache is fetched live, and when that fetch is unavailable and nothing was measured wrong the result is inconclusive rather than passed. What is saved or test-only: the camera pose, the three click points, the hour, and the camera and hit-test seams. When the local pipeline output is missing the test is inconclusive with a message naming the pipeline command; it never passes without that output. A measured missing hit stays a failure even when Esri also reported an outage. What it does not check: water colour or width, the water-surface height, other creeks or hours, the jalama-gauge-reach extent, or whether the modeled elevations are hydrologically right. Imagery dataset used in the visualization: Esri World Imagery.
tests.bugReference: Linear UCS-271 (modeled water stair-stepping and seams, observed Oct 16 2026)
tests.rootCauseAnalysis: Symptom: at a low-flow hour the modeled water shows as short pools at the downstream end of each Creek Segment with dry creek bed between neighbours; at 2022-12-01T12:00Z the thalweg across the 27714637-015/016 junction is dry for 102 m, and on side creek 27714697 in the Dangermond Preserve at 2017-10-01T00:00Z flat water terraces float as separate steps above the sloping bed and the developer clicked three creek-bed points on Creek Segments 043 and 044 with no water-surface hit. Root cause: each Creek Segment's prepared water-surface polygon is one flat terrace at one water-surface elevation (a terrain cell is wet when it lies below the bucket elevation, and every ring vertex gets that same height in the browser), while the creek bed slopes. On the Jalama flowline the median modeled depth is 0.06 m but the bed drops 0.40 m per segment (median) and the thalweg rises 0.33 m inside a segment (median), so water can only cover the downstream end of each segment. The representative bed Stage 1 uses is one cross-section's thalweg rather than the segment's profile: the upstream-most thalweg point sits above the representative bed by 0.61 m at the 90th percentile, so a segment's own upstream thalweg points are dry whenever the depth is shallow. The channel also sits about 6 m off the flowline, so a check on the flowline sees dry ground on both sides at low flow and misses the pattern; this test uses creek-bed points the developer clicked by eye. Future triage: when this fails, compare each segment's bucket elevation with its Stage 1 thalweg elevations upstream of the boundary before suspecting terrain or imagery; a fill that slopes with the bed and per-vertex heights (diagnosis options 1 and 3) is the fix direction.

tests.name: No creek segment stitching failures (cracks between water polygons): At the January 2023 flood peak, neighbouring Creek Segments' modeled water surfaces meet at the same height across their shared boundary, with no step or wall.
tests.methodology: Why it matters: at a flood peak a person should see one water surface flowing down the creek, not a wall where one Creek Segment's water stands above or below its neighbour's. How it checks: opens the locally served page on the “Inferred Creek WSE — hourly (from NOAA National Water Model v3.0 flows)” Dataset for the jalama-gauge-reach extent at 2023-01-10T01:00Z, waits until the test seam reports ready and the modeled seam has finished loading, and checks that the opening time matches the URL. For each of two junctions, 27714637-046/047 and then 27714637-015/016, the test-mode camera command moves the camera instantly to a fixed straight-down pose 130 m above the shared flowline vertex, and the test waits for the modeled loads to finish and for the scene to finish drawing with a still camera. From the developer's local pipeline output (01-cross-sections/cross-sections.json) it joins both segments' Stage 1 thalweg points into one creek-bed line and takes the points 1 m upstream and 1 m downstream of the shared boundary along that line. Each point is projected to a screen pixel and SceneView.hitTest runs there; the nearest water-surface graphic is the surface a viewer sees, and its height is the hit's map-point elevation, with the graphic's bucket minimum as the fallback. The test fails when either Creek Segment shows no water, when either point has no water surface over it, when the two heights differ by more than 0.15 m, or when the downstream height stands more than 0.10 m above the upstream height. The failure message names the junction, the measured heights and difference, the segments and buckets hit, and the drawn surface heights. It then opens the page again on the dangermond-preserve extent at 2023-01-01T11:00Z (Jan 1, 2023, 3:00 AM PST), checks the opening time, moves the camera to the developer's saved oblique pose on side creek 27714669 where a dark seam line and a dry gap crossed the high water, waits for a finished frame, and replays the developer's dev-tools click near Creek Segment 27714669-007: the saved ground point is projected back to a screen pixel and SceneView.hitTest runs there, and the test fails when no water-surface graphic is hit. What is real: the browser page, ArcGIS SceneView, the local pipeline output served by the development middleware, and Esri World Imagery and Esri World Elevation responses reused from the local disk cache; a response missing from the cache is fetched live, and when that fetch is unavailable and nothing was measured wrong the result is inconclusive rather than passed. What is saved or test-only: the developer's seam camera pose, click point, and hour; the camera poses, the two junctions, the hour, and the camera and hit-test seams. When the local pipeline output is missing the test is inconclusive with a message naming the pipeline command; it never passes without that output. A measured step stays a failure even when Esri also reported an outage. What it does not check: water width or overlap at the bend, water colour, continuity along the bed, other junctions, other hours, the Dangermond Preserve extent, or whether the modeled elevations are hydrologically right. Imagery dataset used in the visualization: Esri World Imagery.
tests.bugReference: Linear UCS-271 (modeled water stair-stepping and seams, observed Oct 16 2026)
tests.rootCauseAnalysis: Symptom: at the 2023-01-10T01:00Z flood peak a wall of water stands across the boundary between neighbouring Creek Segments; the 27714637-046 and 047 surfaces differ by 3.05 m against a 1.42 m bed drop, and 015 and 016 by 2.05 m. On side creek 27714669 in the Dangermond Preserve at 2023-01-01T11:00Z the developer saw a dark seam line and a dry gap across high water near Creek Segment 007 and clicked it with no water-surface hit (screenshot on Linear UCS-271). Root cause: Stage 3 solves normal depth for each Creek Segment on its own representative cross-section with no longitudinal continuity, so neighbours' depths disagree (0.08 m at the 90th percentile in normal flow but up to 1.6 m at the peak, with 18% of pairs inverted so downstream water stands higher), and the flat per-segment terraces then meet at different heights. The corridor slabs are also clipped at each segment's own perpendicular, so at a bend (median 16 degrees, 27 degrees at the 90th percentile) the outer side leaves a wedge gap and the inner side overlaps, and the higher terrace shows as a lip. Bucket quantization is at most 0.05 m and is not a cause. Future triage: when this fails, compare the two segments' Stage 3 elevations at that hour with their bed drop before suspecting rendering; one junction elevation shared by both neighbours with a monotone-downstream pass, and corridors clipped at the bend bisector so neighbours share one boundary, is the fix direction (diagnosis options 2 and 3).

tests.name: Clicking a time on the Jalama gauge water-surface elevation chart moves the time slider to that time and redraws the gauge segment's water at that time's elevation.
tests.methodology: Why it matters: a person reads the gauge's water-surface elevation over time on the Water-Surface Elevation Chart, clicks a moment such as a flood peak, and expects the map to jump there. How it checks: opens the locally served observed page in test mode, waits for the test seam and a finished SceneView frame, then moves the camera instantly to a fixed straight-down pose 150 m above the gauge Creek Segment 27714637-026's opening water and settles again. It finds a pixel where SceneView.hitTest reports that segment's water, clear of the sidebar, and clicks it with the real mouse, which selects the segment and fills the chart. It moves the real mouse to the chart line at the committed 2026-01-03T15:15Z flood peak, reads the reading the chart reports under the pointer, and clicks there. The test fails unless the selected time equals that reading's time and lies within about one chart pixel of the peak; the time slider's slot, its spoken value, and the time readout match that time; the gauge segment's water is redrawn at the prepared bucket holding the committed reading for that time, which differs from the opening water; only that segment shows water; and the chart's time cursor sits at that time. What is real: the browser page, ArcGIS SceneView, the committed published creek data, the real mouse clicks, and Esri World Imagery, Esri World Elevation, and USGS 3DEP responses reused from the local disk cache; a response missing from the cache is fetched live and saved, and when that fetch is unavailable and nothing was measured wrong the result is inconclusive rather than passed. What is test-only: the camera command and the read-only seam that reports the selection, chart, slider, and drawn-water state. What it does not check: water colour, the highlight's look, chart styling, keyboard input, or modeled water.

tests.name: Clicking a time on a modeled creek segment's water-surface elevation chart moves the time slider to that time and redraws that segment's modeled water at the charted elevation.
tests.methodology: Why it matters: a person looking at modeled water clicks a moment on a Creek Segment's Water-Surface Elevation Chart and expects the map to show that moment's modeled water. How it checks: opens the locally served page on the “Inferred Creek WSE — hourly (from NOAA National Water Model v3.0 flows)” Dataset for the jalama-gauge-reach extent at 2022-10-01T00:00Z, a low-flow hour, checks that the opening time matches the URL, moves the camera instantly to a fixed straight-down pose 150 m above Creek Segment 27714637-026's opening water, and waits for the modeled loads and a finished frame. It clicks that segment's water with the real mouse at a pixel where SceneView.hitTest reports it, which selects the segment and fills the chart with water year 2023. It moves the real mouse to the chart line at the 2023-01-10T01:00Z flood peak, reads the reading under the pointer, and clicks. The test fails unless the selected time equals that reading's time and lies within 24 hours of the peak; the time slider's slot, spoken value, and readout match it; once the modeled loads finish, the elevation the page holds for the segment equals the charted value; the segment's water is redrawn at the prepared bucket holding that value, which differs from the opening water; and the chart's time cursor sits at that time. What is real: the browser page, ArcGIS SceneView, the developer's local modeled pipeline output served by the development middleware, the real mouse clicks, and Esri World Imagery, Esri World Elevation, and USGS 3DEP responses reused from the local disk cache; a response missing from the cache is fetched live and saved, and when that fetch is unavailable and nothing was measured wrong the result is inconclusive rather than passed. When the local pipeline output is missing the result is inconclusive with a message naming the pipeline command; it never passes without that output. What is test-only: the camera command and the read-only seam. What it does not check: clicks that cross into another water year, water colour or slope, chart styling, other Datasets or extents, or whether the modeled elevations are hydrologically right.

tests.name: Clicking a creek segment highlights only that segment and shows its water-surface elevation chart; clicking another segment moves the highlight and the chart to it.
tests.methodology: Why it matters: a person picks one Creek Segment by clicking its water and needs to see clearly which one is picked, with the old pick released. How it checks: opens the locally served page on the “Inferred Creek WSE — hourly (from NOAA National Water Model v3.0 flows)” Dataset for the jalama-gauge-reach extent at the 2023-01-10T01:00Z flood peak, when neighbouring Creek Segments 27714637-046 and 27714637-047 both show wide water, and checks that nothing is selected or highlighted and the chart is empty. For each segment in turn it moves the camera instantly to a fixed straight-down pose 150 m above that segment's water, waits for the modeled loads and a finished frame, and clicks the segment's water with the real mouse at a pixel where SceneView.hitTest reports it. After each click the test fails unless that segment is the Selected Creek Segment, it is the only segment whose drawn water carries the selection highlight, the chart reports that segment with readings, the chart heading names it, and the chart plot is visible. The second click therefore also checks that the first segment's highlight is gone. What is real: the browser page, ArcGIS SceneView and its highlight, the developer's local modeled pipeline output served by the development middleware, the real mouse clicks, and Esri World Imagery, Esri World Elevation, and USGS 3DEP responses reused from the local disk cache; a response missing from the cache is fetched live and saved, and when that fetch is unavailable and nothing was measured wrong the result is inconclusive rather than passed. When the local pipeline output is missing the result is inconclusive with a message naming the pipeline command. What is test-only: the camera command and the read-only seam that reports the selection and which drawn water graphics carry the highlight. What it does not check: the highlight's colour or pixels, clicking empty ground, observed water, or chart values.

tests.name: Moving the time slider moves the chart's time cursor to the same time.
tests.methodology: Why it matters: during scrubbing or playback a person reads the chart's time cursor to see where the map's moment sits in the record; a cursor that lags or stays put misleads them. How it checks: opens the locally served observed page in test mode, moves the camera instantly to a fixed straight-down pose 150 m above gauge Creek Segment 27714637-026's water, settles the frame, and clicks that segment's water with the real mouse at a pixel where SceneView.hitTest reports it. It checks that the cursor sits at the opening time, then sets the real time slider to the committed 2026-01-03T15:15Z flood peak with the same input and change events a scrub fires. The test fails unless the chart reports its cursor at the flood peak, the drawn cursor line is visible, and the drawn line's horizontal position is within 1 pixel of the chart line's position for that time. What is real: the browser page, ArcGIS SceneView, the committed published creek data, the real mouse click, the real time slider, and Esri World Imagery, Esri World Elevation, and USGS 3DEP responses reused from the local disk cache; a response missing from the cache is fetched live and saved, and when that fetch is unavailable the result is inconclusive rather than passed. What is test-only: the camera command and the read-only seam. What it does not check: Play button playback, modeled water, chart styling, or the water drawn on the map, which FBT-002 covers.

tests.name: Hovering over the chart shows the time and elevation under the pointer without moving the time slider.
tests.methodology: Why it matters: a person sweeps the pointer across the chart to read values before choosing a moment; if hovering changed the time, the map would jump around and lose their place. How it checks: opens the locally served observed page in test mode, moves the camera instantly to a fixed straight-down pose 150 m above gauge Creek Segment 27714637-026's water, settles the frame, and clicks that segment's water with the real mouse at a pixel where SceneView.hitTest reports it. It records the time slider's slot, spoken value, and readout, and the drawn water, then moves the real mouse in steps onto the chart line at the committed 2026-01-03T15:15Z flood peak without clicking and holds it there for 500 ms. The test fails unless the hover readout shows the hovered reading's Pacific time and its committed water-surface elevation to two decimals, and the time slider, spoken value, readout, selected time, drawn water, and chart time cursor are all unchanged. What is real: the browser page, ArcGIS SceneView, the committed published creek data, the real mouse, and Esri World Imagery, Esri World Elevation, and USGS 3DEP responses reused from the local disk cache; a response missing from the cache is fetched live and saved, and when that fetch is unavailable the result is inconclusive rather than passed. What is test-only: the camera command and the read-only seam. What it does not check: touch input, the hover marker's look, modeled water, or what clicking does, which FBT-013 covers.

tests.name: Clicking the map while DevTools are closed, then opening DevTools, shows a yellow ring at that on-map click location; collapsing DevTools removes the ring, and opening DevTools again shows the same ring.
tests.methodology: Why it matters: a person investigating the map opens dev tools and expects the yellow ring to mark the last place they clicked, including a click made before the panel was open, and expects that ring to leave the map when they collapse the panel so it does not cover the creek. How it checks: opens the locally served page on the “Inferred Creek WSE — hourly (from NOAA National Water Model v3.0 flows)” Dataset for the jalama-gauge-reach extent at the 2023-01-10T01:00Z flood peak, with dev tools closed, moves the camera instantly to a fixed straight-down pose 150 m above Creek Segment 27714637-046's water, waits for the modeled loads and a finished frame, and clicks that segment's water with the real mouse at a pixel where SceneView.hitTest reports it. It screenshots a 64×64 pixel crop centered on that click and counts pixels near the marker yellow #f3ef2a (red and green both high and close, blue low), which is distinct from the selection highlight #fbbf24. Pixels inside the sidebar, the dev tools button, or the dev tools panel are ignored. The test fails unless that crop has no marker-yellow pixels while dev tools are closed, at least 8 after the Dev tools button is clicked open, none again after the button collapses the panel, and at least 8 after the button opens the panel again. Each check polls the crop for up to 4 seconds. What is real: the browser page, ArcGIS SceneView, the dev tools toggle and click marker, the developer's local modeled pipeline output served by the development middleware, the real mouse clicks, and Esri World Imagery, Esri World Elevation, and USGS 3DEP responses reused from the local disk cache; a response missing from the cache is fetched live and saved, and when that fetch is unavailable and nothing was measured wrong the result is inconclusive rather than passed. When the local pipeline output is missing the result is inconclusive with a message naming the pipeline command. What is test-only: the camera command and the read-only seam used to find the water pixel. What it does not check: the ring's exact diameter, the dev tools readout text, clicks on empty ground, the observed experience, or the selection highlight, which FBT-015 covers.

tests.name: Zooming the browser in makes the control panel scroll to its last line, and a thin scrollbar shows only while the pointer is over the panel.
tests.methodology: Opens the timeline fixture page with the real control panel markup and stylesheet. The ArcGIS scene and published gauge series are not loaded, and the test fails if the page requests ArcGIS. A 1280×300 window stands in for a zoomed-in browser, which shrinks the page's CSS viewport. There, the panel's last line (the imagery credit) starts below the window edge, the panel stays inside the window, and the panel's own scroll area is taller than it is visible. The test then moves the real mouse over the panel and turns the real wheel, and checks that the scroll offset moves and the credit comes inside the window. For the scrollbar, it reads the panel's computed scrollbar color with the pointer away (thumb transparent), over the panel (thumb visible), and away again (transparent). At a 1280×1600 window the panel has no scroll overflow. It does not check the scrollbar's pixels, its look in Firefox or Safari, touch scrolling, or the map.

tests.name: Playing at 0.5×, 1×, 2×, 5×, and 10× advances the observation slider by about 5, 10, 20, 50, and 100 slots in one second.
tests.methodology: Opens the local page on the timeline fixture while the test server has VITE_TEST_MODE set. That path runs the real Play button, time slider, and speed buttons through the production timeline control, on a 500-slot stand-in clock. The ArcGIS scene, imagery, terrain, and published gauge series are not loaded, and the test fails if the page requests ArcGIS. For each of 0.5×, 1×, 2×, 5×, and 10×, the test pauses, returns the slider to the first slot, clicks that speed button, clicks Play, and reads the slider index at the start and end of one second inside the page. The slot count must sit within 10% of the target for that elapsed time, and the margin is never tighter than one slot, so 1× passes at 9–11 slots in one second. It does not check water, button highlight color, reverse playback, or a chosen calendar date.

tests.name: Highlight the current playback speed, starting at 1× until another speed is chosen.
tests.methodology: Opens the timeline fixture page, waits until the page stylesheet has painted, and reads the computed background, border, and text color of the five speed buttons. Before any click, 1× is the only button whose paint differs. It then clicks 2× and checks that 2× is the only button whose paint differs. The ArcGIS scene and published gauge series are not loaded. It does not press Play, and it does not check how fast the slider moves or the map.

tests.name: Open the Jalama time slider at the first observation slot, not the last.
tests.methodology: Opens the timeline-only page for the real published Jalama record and the app's real opening slot. The 3D scene is not loaded, and the test fails if the page requests ArcGIS. When the time readout leaves the loading text, the slider's slot is 0 and is before the last slot. It does not press Play, and it does not check water, playback speed, or the map.

tests.name: Modeled water-surface elevation validation rejects a value below its Creek Segment's bed.
tests.methodology: Why it matters: modeled water below a Creek Segment's bed is physically impossible, and if it reached the browser it would draw water under the ground or no water where some is expected. The final validation step of the modeled water-surface elevation pipeline (Stage 5) is the last guard before that data is used, so this test makes sure the guard actually trips. How it checks: the test builds a tiny synthetic fixture in a temporary directory: two made-up Creek Segments with bed elevations of 100 m and 50 m, matching cross-section and polygon-ladder records, and one Time Series file of three monthly values per segment listed in a one-Dataset catalog. It calls the real Stage 5 validation function, validateModeledWaterSurfaceElevationOutputs, twice. First with values that are all at or above the bed, including one exactly at the bed and one missing value; every check must pass. Then with one value 0.1 m below the 100 m bed; only the bed check may fail, with exactly one violation whose message names that Time Series file, that Creek Segment (and not the other one), the timestamp, the value, and the bed. What is real: the validation code and its check names. What is synthetic: every input file; nothing is read from real pipeline output, and there is no network. What it does not check: whether real modeled values are correct, the hydraulics that produced them, the other validation checks, or how Stage 5 writes its catalog and report files.

tests.name: Every Creek Segment's rating curve gives a higher or equal discharge as water-surface elevation rises.
tests.methodology: Why it matters: the modeled pipeline turns discharge (flow) into water-surface elevation by reading a rating curve backwards. If a curve's discharge ever fell as the water rose, a rising flow could map to a lower water surface, and modeled water on screen would drop while the creek floods. This happens in real cross-sections where water first spills onto a flat bench: the wetted perimeter jumps while the wet area barely grows, so raw Manning's-equation discharge dips. Stage 2 fixes that by keeping a running maximum of discharge, and this test protects that fix. How it checks: it builds two synthetic representative cross-sections with 1 m sample spacing. One has a narrow 1 m deep channel and a wide flat bench on each side; the other is a plain V-shaped channel with no bench. It runs the real Stage 2 rating-curve builder, buildRatingCurveRecord, on each, then checks that every curve has more than 50 ladder steps, that water-surface elevation strictly rises step to step, and that published discharge never decreases. To prove the bench fixture really reaches the bad case, it also checks that the bench curve climbs more than 0.5 m above the bench, that its raw Manning discharge does fall at least once, and that Stage 2 flags the held steps as non-monotonic-discharge, while the plain channel's raw discharge never falls. What is real: the rating-curve code, Manning's roughness and ladder settings, and the wetted-geometry math. What is synthetic: both cross-sections; no real terrain, pipeline output, or network is used. What it does not check: whether the real Jalama rating curves are accurate, the choice of roughness or slope, inversion from discharge to water-surface elevation, or rendering.

tests.name: Rebuilding the published creek visualization data from retained source snapshots reproduces the shipped files byte for byte.
tests.methodology: Why it matters: the observed Jalama gauge water that the app ships is built by the publish pipeline from committed source snapshots. Modeled-water work reuses and refactors shared code such as Creek Segment cutting and corridor measurement. This test makes sure such a change cannot silently alter the observed water people already see. How it checks: it calls the real publish function, publishCreekVisualizationData, offline, writing into a fresh temporary directory, and also redirects the reviewed station-assignment file there, so nothing in the app's public folder or the retained source folder is touched. The inputs are the committed retained snapshots: the TNC flowline, the USGS 11120600 station and observations, the USGS 3DEP 1 m elevation window, and the reviewed snapshot of the modeled pipeline's Stage 4 polygon set for the gauge's Creek Segment (WSE Polygon Generation Method junction-sloped-terrain-fill v1). Observed water-surface polygons are copied from that Stage 4 snapshot, not traced by publish; the elevation window is used only to measure the corridor the release validation checks the copied polygons against. It then compares the set of rebuilt file names with the published files tracked by Git, and the SHA-256 hash of each rebuilt file with that file's content at the current Git commit (HEAD). Comparing with HEAD rather than the working copy means an uncommitted republish cannot make the test agree with itself. A deliberate data change therefore fails this test until the new published files are committed. What is real: the whole publish pipeline, its validation, and the committed snapshots and published files. Nothing is mocked except silencing console output, and there is no network. What it does not check: whether the source snapshots are still current with USGS or TNC, how the browser draws the files, the reviewed station-assignment file's contents, or modeled water.

tests.name: The observed gauge segment's published water polygons are identical to the modeled Stage 4 polygons for that segment.
tests.methodology: Why it matters: observed and modeled water must draw one set of prepared water-surface polygons, so switching between the Jalama gauge readings and a modeled Dataset never changes the water's shape at the same water-surface elevation. Publish copies a reviewed, committed snapshot of Stage 4's polygon set for the gauge's Creek Segment, 27714637-026, so a drifted snapshot or a newer Stage 4 run that nobody re-reviewed would quietly split them again. How it checks: it reads the snapshot's provenance file to find the Stage 4 source path and method (junction-sloped-terrain-fill v1), then reads the 27714637-026 polygon set from three places: the local Stage 4 output for the jalama-gauge-reach extent, the published water-surface-polygon-sets.json, and the retained snapshot. Each must hold exactly one set for that Creek Segment. The published set and the retained set must each deep-equal the Stage 4 set: segmentNetworkVersion, segment id, and every bucket's minimum, maximum, and ring coordinates. When the gitignored local Stage 4 output is missing, the test is skipped with a message naming npm run pipeline:modeled-wse:all -- --extent=jalama-gauge-reach; a skip is reported as not run, never passed. What is real: the committed published file, the committed snapshot and provenance, and the developer's local Stage 4 output. Nothing is mocked, nothing is rebuilt, and there is no network. What it does not check: whether Stage 4's polygons are hydraulically right, other Creek Segments, the dangermond-preserve extent, how the browser draws the polygons, or that the published file is reproducible from retained sources (FST-003 does).

tests.name: The catalog rejects a test entry that breaks the classification rules, and feature filters return each matching test once.
tests.methodology: Builds a sample catalog in memory, breaks one classification rule at a time, and checks that validation names that break, including a malformed catalog test identifier and a category prefix that does not match its category. It also checks that a feature filter returns each matching sample once, and that asking for one catalog test identifier still returns that test when it is disabled. With synthetic Playwright JSON, it checks that the stored result is the final attempt: a later pass after an earlier failure or inconclusive attempt is passed with a passed-after-retry record, a single pass has no flag, a final failure stays failed, and a final inconclusive attempt stays inconclusive. It also checks the stored error log: a final failure keeps the final attempt's number, error location, trace path, and screenshot path; a pass after retry keeps the last failed attempt's log; and stored log text has no ANSI color codes and stays within the line and character caps in failure-log.ts. It does not open the catalog page, require the live catalog to contain zero tests, or run an application test. It checks that a Bug Check requires a nonempty bug reference and root cause analysis on a Feature Behavior Test, and that a baseline test leaves both null.

tests.name: The release check runs the core tests first and stops before feature tests if a core test fails.
tests.methodology: Calls the same release-gate function the release command uses, with stand-in results. It checks that core runs first and that a failing or inconclusive core result stops the feature phase. It does not run the application or a real failing core test.
